text: You just touched one memory address. Spatial locality says the next touch is usually a {{c1::nearby}} address. Temporal locality says you will reuse the {{c2::same}} spot soon.
extra: A walk through a contiguous array is the textbook spatial case: z[i] then z[i+1].

text: Lay your data out as a flat contiguous array and you get strong {{c1::spatial locality}}, because successive elements sit next to each other and often share a cache line.
extra: Pointer chasing jumps around memory, so the cache helps much less.

text: Need to ship a big buffer over MPI or copy it to a GPU? One contiguous block can move as {{c1::one}} message or copy. Scattered pointer data cannot.
extra: That is why flat buffers matter for transfers, not only for cache hits.

text: C stores 2D arrays in {{c1::row-major}} order. For \(y[i]+=A[i][j]*x[j]\), nest with outer \(i\) and inner \(j\) and you get {{c2::far fewer}} cache misses than outer \(j\) inner \(i\).
extra: Outer-i walks each row contiguously. Outer-j strides down a column and thrashing starts.

text: Flynn calls classical von Neumann {{c1::SISD}}: one instruction stream working on one data stream.
extra: One instruction at a time, a few data items per instruction.

text: Flynn {{c1::SIMD}} means one control unit broadcasts the same instruction to many datapaths, each with its own data.
extra: On a data-dependent if, lanes that fail the predicate sit idle while the others work.

text: Flynn {{c1::MISD}} is multiple instruction streams on a single data stream. It is rare, but it fills out the taxonomy.
extra: The four boxes you need for M2 are SISD, SIMD, MISD, and MIMD.

text: Flynn {{c1::MIMD}} means multiple instruction streams and multiple data streams. Think independent cores that usually run asynchronously.
extra: This is the usual multicore and cluster model.

text: A vector processor works on {{c1::vectors}} with vector registers and vector instructions. A conventional CPU works on {{c2::scalars}} one element at a time.
extra: Same op applied elementwise, so it is SIMD-style. Systems also add interleaved memory, strided access, and scatter/gather.

text: Vector machines shine because {{c1::vectorizing compilers}} are strong, memory {{c2::bandwidth}} is very high, and every loaded item actually gets used.
extra: Cache machines may pull a whole line and leave some words untouched. Vectors load what they need.

text: Vector machines struggle with {{c1::irregular}} data structures, hit a wall on {{c2::vector-length}} scaling, and need expensive custom long-vector hardware.
extra: Real systems usually scale by adding more vector processors, not by making each vector longer.

text: Shared-memory MIMD: cores coordinate {{c1::implicitly}} by touching shared data. Distributed-memory MIMD: each core has private memory and coordinates {{c2::explicitly}} with messages.
extra: Shared means every core can reach each location. Distributed means you talk over an interconnect.
